summary: For ages 8-9, press repeated reasoning into justified generalisation: not just noticing that 3×4=12, 3×40=120, 3×400=1200 scale by ten, but saying WHY (place value shifts the digits one place) and testing whether a rule always holds. Similarly, families of equivalent fractions (1/2, 2/4, 3/6) reveal a numerator-half-denominator pattern that should be tested on new cases, not trusted on sight. Name 'derive from a known fact' (8×7 = 8×5 + 8×2) as a reusable strategy the child can describe in their own words. The target is the justification and the extension, not just correct numbers.
misconceptions: Uses 'add a zero' for ×10 scaling with no place-value reason, so it fails on decimals
Notices a pattern but treats it as coincidence, unable to say why it must hold or whether it always will
Over-generalises the 1/2 rule to other fractions, or applies it without testing
Derives a fact but does not recognise the derive-from-known-facts move as a general strategy for other facts

activities.title: Scaling machine with a 'why' window
steps: Start from 3×4 = 12, then produce 3×40 and 3×400 by scaling up by ten each step
For each step, explain WHY the product gets ten times bigger using place value (40 is ten times 4, so the answer is ten times bigger; the digits shift one place left) rather than saying 'add a zero'
Predict 3×4000 and state whether the same reason guarantees it will work, then check
Now test the idea going the OTHER way: 0.4 is a tenth of 4, so is 3×0.4 a tenth of 12? Work it out and explain why the place value, not an added zero, decides this
activities.insight: The product scales by ten BECAUSE place value shifts the digits one column, so the pattern must keep working (including for 3×4000). Reasoning from place value (not just appending zeros) also handles decimal cases like 3×0.4 = 1.2 — here 0.4 is a tenth of 4, so the product is a tenth of 12, with the digits shifting one column right. The add-a-zero shortcut cannot explain this, and it gives wrong answers for decimals (1.2 × 10 is 12, not 1.20).

activities.title: Equivalent-fraction family tester
steps: Line up 1/2, 2/4, 3/6 on a fraction bar or number line (same whole) and notice that each numerator is half its denominator
State the candidate rule 'a fraction equals 1/2 when the numerator is half the denominator'
Invent a new fraction and test whether the rule holds by checking it against the bar/number line, not by eyeballing
Try a trap case: is 5/9 equivalent to 1/2 because 5 is 'about half' of 9? How could you be sure?
activities.insight: A noticed rule must be tested before it is trusted; the numerator-half-denominator pattern for 1/2 can be confirmed on a model, and over-applying it (e.g. to 5/9) is caught by checking rather than guessing.

activities.title: Derive-from-known-facts as a named strategy
steps: Work out 8×7 from facts you already know: 8×5 = 40 and 8×2 = 16, then add to get 56
Explain why splitting 7 into 5 + 2 lets you reuse known facts (an array or area model split into an 8×5 part and an 8×2 part)
Describe the move in your own words as a general strategy for any hard table fact
Try the same strategy on another fact (e.g. 6×7 or 9×6) and say which known facts you'd lean on
activities.insight: Deriving an unknown fact by splitting a factor and reusing known facts is a reusable general strategy, not a one-off; the child should recognise and name it so they can apply it to other facts.

activities.title: Prove it holds every time
steps: After extending a scaling chain or stating a fraction rule, answer: how could you convince someone the pattern works every time, not just for these three cases?
Produce a test case for any stated rule ('does it still work for 3×4000? for 4/8?') and report what you find
Distinguish a justified generalisation ('it must, because place value shifts') from a guess ('it just seems to')
activities.insight: A pattern noticed is not a pattern proven; a reason it must hold, plus a fresh test case, separates a reliable generalisation from a coincidence.

activities.title: Check your generalisation (quick questions)
steps: Continue the scaling chain: given 3×4=12 and 3×40=120, give 3×400 and 3×4000
Pick which fractions are equivalent to 1/2 from a set that includes near-misses (e.g. 5/9)
Choose the correct derivation of 8×7 and reject the wrong split 8×5 + 2 in favour of 8×5 + 8×2 = 56
For each choice, say WHY it is correct, not just which answer
activities.insight: Selecting correct continuations and derivations, paired with a stated reason, confirms the child is generalising with justification rather than pattern-matching.

checkQuestion: You know 3 × 4 = 12. What are 3 × 40 and 3 × 400? Explain WHY the pattern works — and would it still work for 3 × 4000?
checkAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for 120 and 1200 with a place-value justification ('40 is ten times 4, so the answer is ten times bigger; the digits shift a place') and confidence it extends to 3×4000 = 12000 for the same reason. The WHY and the extension, not just the numbers, are the target.
